title: Temporary Protected Status needs to be protected from political whims
summary: Temporary may be part of the the title, but temporary protected status for immigrants shouldn't be arbitrary, write Jennica Larrison and Ben Coleman, who say a White House push to cancel TPS for a dozen countries is "nothing short of betrayal."
content:
by Jennica Larrison and Ben Coleman, Maryland Matters June 15, 2026

by Jennica Larrison and Ben Coleman, Maryland Matters June 15, 2026

Our neighbors hold jobs, pay taxes, raise children in Maryland schools, and contribute billions to the U.S. economy. They are also one court decision away from being told to leave. The Trump administration, as part of its immigration policies, has attempted to cancel temporary protected status [TPS] for more than a dozen countries.

On April 29, the Supreme Court heard arguments in the case of Trump v. Miot, that will decide the fate of TPS for Haitian and Syrian nationals. Running concurrently through the courts is the case of African Communities Together v. Markwayne Mullin, which addresses the fate of TPS for Somali immigrants. Maryland Attorney General Brown joined 15 other state attorneys general this spring to defend TPS status for Somali immigrants.

The vulnerability of TPS should be urgently fortified with clearer guidelines for cancellation and a path to long-term residency. Otherwise, the cruel and sudden prospect of statelessness and deportation for thousands working and living in Maryland will continue to plague communities across the state and fuel the chaos of immigration enforcement.

The TPS program was designed to give deportation protections to individuals already living in the U.S., whose country of origin is deemed by the Department of Homeland Security as unsafe for their return. But the parameters for designating safe and unsafe countries of origin are vague and subjective, leaving the policy and people’s lives and communities in the hands of the DHS secretary.

Maryland is home to over 33,000 TPS holders, ranking 10th in the country for most TPS residents. TPS holders in Maryland are historically from El Salvador and more recently from Venezuela, Syria, Haiti and Somalia. Individuals are deeply embedded in Maryland communities and its labor market, particularly in Prince George’s and Montgomery counties, where TPS holders work in healthcare, hospitality, construction, transportation, public service and more.

Past research has shown that over 17,000 children born in Maryland have parents who hold TPS status. The revocation of status will affect Marylanders in multiple aspects of their daily lives.

This concern is not hyperbole but rooted in the administration’s actions. Prior to a pause in the district court on Feb. 2, TPS for Haitian nationals was set to expire on Feb. 3. Reports about immigration enforcement operations that were due to ramp up on Feb. 4, targeting areas like Springfield, Ohio, were causing anxiety and speculation among the large Haitian population there.

The timing of the planned ICE raids coinciding with the expiration of TPS raises questions about profiteering and the deportation industrial complex as well as the whimsical nature of the program.

Yemen recently joined a growing list of countries like Haiti, Venezuela, Syria, Somalia and others facing TPS cancellation. Despite a purge of immigration judges, district courts across the country agree that these countries are all still plagued by severe destabilization and violence. Deporting people back to their country of origin or to other states, under an expanding list of transactional third-country agreements like Cameroon and El Salvador and its notorious CECOT prison, betrays the notion of humanitarian assistance and solidarity.

The Trump administration’s actions spotlight the TPS program’s vulnerabilities. The policy is highly vulnerable to shifting political moods by design and has been used by several administrations to increase or decrease migrant numbers based on economic or political calculations without consideration of the human cost of those living under a precarious immigration status.

However, TPS holders participate in the labor force at higher rates than U.S. citizens, and contribute billions of dollars to the economy every year. People who lose TPS status are also at risk of losing access to health care. A plan to extend access to Maryland’s health exchange program to undocumented migrants has been delayed until at least 2028.

Congress should introduce pathways to long-term residency and add clear parameters for designation and cancellation. Not only would this curb the ideological whims of changing administrations and provide stability for individuals under temporary protective status, but it would also provide social and economic security in the communities where individuals reside.

Allowing people to live, work, and invest in communities for years only to have the rug pulled out from under them is nothing short of betrayal, with the human cost too high for anyone who believes in the right to life and dignity.
